signals.title: Are the newest chips still scarce?
signals.value_label: 3-month change in rent, H200 and B200
signals.now: Rents on Nvidia's newest chips are still climbing: buyers are competing for a limited supply.
signals.rule: Turns when the 3-month change drops below -5%. Watch when it is between -5% and +5%, or the last month is negative.
signals.why: Rising rents on the newest chips are the cleanest sign that demand exceeds supply. When they roll over, the shortage that justifies record capex is ending.

signals.title: Are older chips losing value?
signals.now: H100 rent is still rising: even 2023-era chips are in demand.
signals.rule: Turns when H100 rent falls more than 10% over 3 months. Watch when it is flat or falling.
signals.why: The H100 is the most widely installed AI chip. An oversupply shows up here first, and it hits the balance sheets of companies that borrowed to buy H100 fleets.
signals.extra: Cost per unit of work, H100 vs B200: 0.78. Above 1.00 means an H100 costs more per unit of work than the newer B200, the point where operators retire H100s. Provisional: the performance factor behind it is not yet sourced.

signals.title: Is AI getting cheaper faster than the chips?
signals.value_label: AI output price vs chip rent, 3 months
signals.now: Over 3 months the price of open-model AI output fell 59% while chip rents rose 28% (average of H100, H200, B200). A chip-hour whose output sold for $1.00 three months ago now sells for $0.41, while the chip-hour costs 28% more to rent.
signals.rule: Watch while the gap is above 30 points: someone in the middle is absorbing it. Turns when chip rents start falling too: the squeeze then shifts from AI sellers to chip owners.
signals.why: Cheaper AI drives more usage, which is the bull case for chip demand. But a company that rents chips and sells AI output at falling prices sees margins shrink unless efficiency keeps up.

signals.title: How hard must each chip work to pay its rent?
signals.value_label: AI tokens one H100 must produce per hour to cover rent
signals.now: At today's prices an H100 must produce about 42 million tokens an hour (≈11,728 per second, nonstop) just to cover its rent. That is +163% since 2026-07-22.
signals.rule: Turns when the break-even rate exceeds what a chip can actually produce. No published benchmark is logged yet, so this can only flag the trend: watch when the requirement rises 50%+.
signals.why: This is the squeeze in one number. If the tokens a chip must sell rise faster than software and new hardware can deliver, serving AI on rented chips stops paying.
signals.short: Work each chip must do to pay rent

exposure.label: Selling AI output against this break-even

signals.title: Does the market expect cheaper chips later?
signals.now: Renting an H100 today costs 1.89× the reported 5-year contract rate. Buyers pay a premium for chips now, which says the market expects rents to fall. Long contracts are also cheaper for volume and credit reasons, so the trend in this ratio matters more than its level. One unverified data point so far, so no call.
signals.rule: Turns when today's rent falls to within 10% of long-term contract rents: the shortage premium is gone.
signals.why: The premium of spot over long contracts measures how much of today's price is shortage. It shrinks before rents fall outright.

signals.title: Is Big Tech still accelerating spending?
signals.value_label: Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta capex vs a year earlier (2026-06-30)
signals.now: Combined capex was $165B last quarter, +87% on a year ago, and the growth rate is still rising (+80% the quarter before).
signals.rule: Watch when the growth rate is lower than the quarter before in two of the last three quarters: spending still rises but the acceleration is fading. Turns when spending falls below the year before.
signals.why: Chipmaker revenue follows the change in capex, not its level. In 2022 growth slowed from +30% to +7% over three quarters; this rule flagged it at Q4 2022, one quarter before spending fell in 2023.

signals.title: Is power becoming the bottleneck?
signals.value_label: 12-month growth in grid load, PJM (Virginia–Ohio) / ERCOT (Texas)
signals.now: Electricity use on the two grids with the most data center construction is growing +4.1% (PJM) and +5.1% (ERCOT) a year. For most of the 2010s US demand barely grew, so this is new load. Industrial power prices in the big data-center states are +7.0% on a year ago (median of 5 states, led by OH +26% and VA +9%; US average +6.6%), 12-month average to 2026-08.
signals.rule: Tightening when either grid's load grows more than 3% a year, or the median industrial price in data-center states rises more than 5%. Binding when both happen.
signals.why: If power, not chips, limits how many chips can be switched on, the shortage lasts longer: chips can't flood the market faster than grids connect them. That supports chip rents and favors power-efficient new chips, but it caps how many chips get installed.
signals.extra: Data-center states: VA, OH, TX, GA, AZ. EIA price data runs about three months behind.

all.name: Demand outrunning supply
all.plain: AI is getting cheaper to buy, yet renting the chips that make it costs more. Usage is growing faster than chips can be built.
all.means: Chip owners keep pricing power. The squeeze lands on the companies that rent chips and sell AI output at falling prices.

all.name: Rents have stopped rising
all.plain: AI keeps getting cheaper, but chip rents have gone flat. The shortage is no longer getting worse.
all.means: Often the step between a shortage and a glut. Watch whether rents tip down next.

all.name: Supply catching up
all.plain: AI prices and chip rents are both falling. Enough chips are now online that owners compete on price.
all.means: The shortage is over. In past chip cycles this preceded capex cuts and falling chip orders.

all.name: Shortage passed to customers
all.plain: Chip rents are rising and AI prices have stopped falling. Sellers are passing higher costs on.
all.means: AI sellers have pricing power; demand is strong enough to absorb it.

all.name: Customers paying more for everything
all.plain: AI prices and chip rents are both rising.
all.means: Strongest demand reading. Rare so far.

scenario.rule: 3-month change in open-model AI price vs average H100/H200/B200 rent; moves under +5% count as flat.

tripwires.name: AI price outruns rent by 30 pts

verdict.text: Shortage intact. Sellers of AI output are being squeezed. Power is the binding limit. Nearest turn: H100 rent drops 10% in 3 months (now +13%, trigger −10%, 23 pts to go).
